name: Indra Jatra
when: September, eight days in the lunar month of Yanla (Bhadra)
summary: Kathmandu's great street festival, Yenya in Nepal Bhasa: eight days of masked dances, a tall pole raised at Hanuman Dhoka, the giant mask of Seto Bhairab pouring rice beer, and the chariot procession of the Kumari, the living goddess. The old city is taken over by its own people.
body: Indra Jatra opens when a tall wooden pole, the yosin or lingo, is raised in front of the old palace at Hanuman Dhoka, flying Indra's banner. For eight days, Kathmandu's Durbar Square and old neighbourhoods fill with masked dancers: the red-faced Lakhe leaping through the streets, Pulukisi, the elephant Indra rode, and the dancing gods of the Devi pyakhan. Images of Indra, arms outstretched as if bound, are set up on platforms across the city.

On the third day, the Kumari leaves her house in a three-tiered chariot, followed by two smaller chariots carrying boys who embody Ganesh and Bhairav. Thousands of people pull and follow them through the old city over three days of processions. At Hanuman Dhoka, the great gilded mask of Seto Bhairab is uncovered, and rice beer flows from its mouth through a pipe; catching a sip is said to bring luck.

The festival also remembers the dead. On Upaku wanegu, families who lost someone in the past year walk the old city's boundaries with incense and lamps. It was during Indra Jatra in 1768 that Prithvi Narayan Shah entered Kathmandu and took the throne. Today, the head of state attends the Kumari Jatra and receives a tika from the living goddess, continuing a royal tradition.
tips: For the Kumari chariot procession, find a step on a temple plinth in Basantapur at least an hour before it starts.
Keep valuables minimal and agree a meeting point; the crowds in the Durbar Square are dense.
Do not photograph the Kumari with flash, and follow police instructions about where you may stand.

faqs.a: Indra Jatra falls in the lunar month of Yanla, usually in September, and lasts eight days. The exact dates change each year with the Nepali calendar. The Kumari Jatra, the chariot procession of the living goddess, starts on the third day. Check current status before you travel and book Kathmandu hotels early.

The festival begins with the raising of a tall pole at Hanuman Dhoka. Over eight days, masked dancers perform in the streets, the giant Seto Bhairab mask pours rice beer, images of Indra are displayed, and the Kumari is pulled through the old city in her chariot. Families also remember those who died in the past year.

faqs.q: Can tourists see the Kumari at Indra Jatra?
faqs.a: Yes. During the Kumari Jatra, the living goddess rides in a chariot through the old city over three days, and crowds line the streets to see her. It is one of the few times she leaves her house. Arrive early for a good spot near Basantapur, and never photograph her with flash.

faqs.q: What is the legend of Indra Jatra?
faqs.a: Local legend says Indra, king of the gods, came to the valley to steal parijat flowers for his mother. He was caught and tied up as a common thief. His mother came looking for him, and when people learned who he was, they released him. In return, she promised mist and dew for the winter crops.

name: Gai Jatra
when: August or September, the day after Janai Purnima
summary: The festival of cows, held the day after Janai Purnima, when families who lost a member in the past year parade a cow, or a child dressed as one, through the old towns. It mixes grief and humour, and in Bhaktapur becomes a week of processions and stick dances.
body: Gai Jatra is about death and laughter at once. Hindu belief holds that cows help guide the souls of the dead, so families who have lost someone in the past year join a procession through their town with a cow, or a boy dressed as a cow with a painted mask, horns and a garland. Neighbours give food, coins and fruit to the participants. Walking together, families see they are not alone in their grief.

In Kathmandu, tradition credits King Pratap Malla with adding humour to the day. His queen was inconsolable after the death of their son, so he asked people to come out in costume and make jokes, promising a reward to anyone who could make her smile. Gai Jatra has since become a day of satire, when comedians and newspapers mock politicians and public figures.

Bhaktapur celebrates Gai Jatra on the largest scale. Families build tall bamboo frames, called taahamacha, dressed in cloth and decorated with a photograph of the deceased, and carry them round the town. Men dance the ghinta ghisi, a stick dance, through the streets for days after. It is one of the best times to see Bhaktapur's festival life.
tips: Bhaktapur's Gai Jatra is longer and more theatrical than Kathmandu's; stay in the old town if you can.
Remember that families are mourning; be respectful with cameras and do not get in the way of processions.
Monsoon rain is likely, so carry a light rain jacket and shoes with grip.

faqs.a: Gai Jatra falls on the day after Janai Purnima, the full moon of the month of Shrawan or Bhadra, usually in August or early September. In Bhaktapur, related processions and stick dances continue for about a week. Dates change each year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Why do people dress as cows on Gai Jatra?
faqs.a: Hindu belief holds that cows help guide the souls of the dead. Families who lost someone in the past year send a cow, or a child dressed as one, in a procession through the town. It honours the dead and helps the living share their grief with the community.

faqs.q: Where is the best place to see Gai Jatra?
faqs.a: Bhaktapur, where the festival is celebrated on the largest scale, with tall decorated frames, costumed processions and the ghinta ghisi stick dance. Kathmandu's old city also has processions and satirical performances. Patan and Kirtipur hold their own versions.

faqs.q: Is Gai Jatra a sad festival?
faqs.a: It is both sad and joyful. Families remember relatives who died in the past year, but the day is also full of humour, costumes and satire, a tradition credited to King Pratap Malla. Visitors usually find the mix moving. Be respectful of families taking part.

name: Bisket Jatra
summary: Bhaktapur's New Year festival: the chariot of Bhairav is hauled through the town in a tug of war between upper and lower halves, a tall pole is raised and pulled down to mark the new year, and nearby Thimi throws clouds of vermilion. Loud, crowded and full of energy.
body: Bisket Jatra runs for about nine days around Nepali New Year in mid-April. It begins in Taumadhi, beside Nyatapola, where the huge three-roofed chariot of Bhairav is assembled. Men from the upper and lower halves of the town grab thick ropes at either end and pull in opposite directions; the winning side takes the chariot into its own quarter. A smaller chariot carries the goddess Bhadrakali.

Outside the town, at a field by the river, a tall wooden pole, the yosin or lingo, is raised with two long banners. On the evening before New Year, crowds pull it down, and its fall marks the start of the new year. The festival's name is often traced to a Newar phrase about killing snakes, recalled in the banners said to represent two serpents.

The day after New Year, neighbouring Thimi celebrates Sindure Jatra, with palanquins of gods spun through the streets and clouds of orange vermilion thrown by everyone. In nearby Bode, a volunteer has his tongue pierced with a needle and walks the village carrying a ring of lamps. Bisket is the best time to see Bhaktapur's people at full volume.
tips: Watch the chariot tug of war from a raised step or a rooftop cafe, not from the street; the chariot can lurch suddenly.
Wear old clothes for Sindure Jatra in Thimi, and protect cameras and phones from vermilion powder.
Book Bhaktapur rooms weeks ahead for New Year; the old town fills up.

faqs.a: Bisket Jatra takes place over about nine days around Nepali New Year, Baisakh 1, which usually falls on 13 or 14 April. The pole is pulled down on the evening before New Year, and Sindure Jatra in Thimi follows the next day. Check current status before you travel.

The chariot of Bhairav is hauled through Bhaktapur in a tug of war between the upper and lower halves of town, a tall pole is raised and pulled down to mark the new year, and the goddess Bhadrakali's chariot joins the processions. Nearby towns hold their own events, including Sindure Jatra in Thimi.

faqs.q: Is Bisket Jatra safe for tourists?
faqs.a: Generally yes, if you keep a safe distance from the chariots and ropes. The chariot tug of war is rough, and the chariot can tilt or swing suddenly, so watch from steps, rooftops or the edges of the square. Keep valuables minimal and avoid the densest crowds with children.

faqs.q: What is the legend of Bisket Jatra?
faqs.a: Local legend tells of a princess whose husbands each died on their wedding night. A brave prince stayed awake and saw two serpents emerge from her nostrils, and killed them. The festival's name is often explained as snake slaying, and the two banners on the pole are said to represent the snakes.

name: Rato Machhindranath Jatra
when: Late April to June, starting in the month of Baisakh
summary: The longest chariot festival in Nepal: Patan's rain god, Bunga Dyah, rides a towering chariot of wood and cane, about 60 ft tall, pulled through the city's streets over several weeks. It ends at Jawalakhel with the Bhoto Jatra, when a jewelled vest is held up to the crowd.
body: The festival honours Rato Machhindranath, the red Karunamaya, god of rain and harvest, who spends half of each year in Bungamati and half in Patan. In spring, after the god is bathed in a public ceremony, his chariot is built at Pulchowk by hereditary craftsmen, using timber, cane and rope, with a tall spire bound in green branches. It is about 60 ft high and takes weeks to build.

Then the chariot is pulled through Patan in stages, often over a month or more, via Gabahal, Sundhara and Lagankhel towards Jawalakhel. Hundreds of men haul on the ropes while the chariot sways above the crowds, and a smaller chariot of Minnath follows. Progress depends on the omens, the weather and the strength of the pullers, and the chariot sometimes stops for days.

At Jawalakhel comes the Bhoto Jatra. Legend tells of a dispute over a jewelled vest between a farmer and a serpent; the god has kept it ever since, and once a year an official holds it up from the chariot so its owner may claim it. The head of state traditionally attends. Afterwards the god is taken to Bungamati, and in every twelfth year the festival starts from there.
tips: Ask us for the current position of the chariot each day; it moves in stages and can pause for days.
Keep well clear of the chariot wheels and ropes; the chariot is heavy and can swing without warning.
Walk rather than drive in Patan during the festival, as roads round the chariot are closed.

faqs.q: When is the Rato Machhindranath festival?
faqs.a: It begins in the month of Baisakh, usually late April or May, and the chariot moves through Patan over several weeks. It ends at Jawalakhel with the Bhoto Jatra, which can fall in May or June. Dates follow the lunar calendar and astrologers' advice, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How tall is the Rato Machhindranath chariot?
faqs.a: The main chariot stands about 60 ft, or roughly 18 m, high, with a tall spire of branches above the shrine. It is built each year at Pulchowk from timber, cane and rope by hereditary craftsmen. A smaller chariot carries Minnath, who travels with Rato Machhindranath.

Bhoto Jatra is the final event of the festival at Jawalakhel, when an official holds up a jewelled vest, the bhoto, from the chariot for the crowd to see. Legend says the vest's ownership was disputed between a farmer and a serpent, and the god keeps it until its true owner claims it.

faqs.q: Can visitors help pull the Rato Machhindranath chariot?
faqs.a: The pulling is done mainly by local men organised by the festival's guthis, and the chariot is very heavy and can be dangerous. Visitors usually watch from the side. If locals invite you to join on the ropes at a quiet moment, follow their lead closely and stay away from the wheels.
